item.title: US prepared for protracted stalemate with Iran
item.itunes:title: US prepared for protracted stalemate with Iran
item.description:
Global stocks sold off as AI spending fears flare up, Brazilians will vote this weekend in a close presidential race, and the US is prepared for a lengthy stalemate in the war with Iran. Plus, how banks are reacting to a potential tax rise from UK chancellor John Healey, and why are western pharmaceutical companies heading to China?


Mentioned in this podcast:

Meta sell-off drags US tech stocks lower as AI spending fears flare up

US prepared for protracted Iran stalemate

Should UK banks be taxed more?

Lula turns to selfie videos in Brazil election fightback

Flávio Bolsonaro, scion of a Brazilian political dynasty now eyeing victory

China’s rapid human trials draw western drugmakers — and safety concerns


Want to get in touch? Email us at podcasts@ft.com


Note: The FT does not use generative AI to voice its podcasts


The FT News Briefing is produced by Sonja Hutson, Saffeya Ahmed, and Josh Gabert-Doyon. Our editor is Marc Filippino. Our video producer is Zachary Alfred. Our show is mixed by Sam Giovinco and Alex Higgins. Additional help from Gavin Kallmann, Michael Lello, Vanessa Brown, Peter Barber and David da Silva. Our executive producer is Topher Forhecz. Flo Phillips is the FT’s global head of audio. The show’s theme music is by Metaphor Music.

item.title: Elon Musk’s $3.6tn gamble to merge SpaceX and Tesla
item.itunes:title: Elon Musk’s $3.6tn gamble to merge SpaceX and Tesla
item.itunes:subtitle: The world’s richest man attempts his most audacious deal yet. But shareholders and global regulators will need convincing
item.description:
Meta plans to create a new class of non-voting shares, Mathias Döpfner, chief executive and co-owner of Germany’s Axel Springer, has sought to acquire a stake in TikTok’s European operations, and US envoy Steve Witkoff discussed resuming peace talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine. Plus, can Elon Musk pull off a merger of SpaceX and Tesla?


Mentioned in this podcast:

Meta to create new non-voting share class

Tesla’s profits slip on weaker vehicle sales

Politico and Telegraph owner pitched deal to buy European arm of TikTok

Rockets, robots and risk: Elon Musk’s $3.6tn gamble to merge Tesla and SpaceX

What Elon Musk stands to gain from a Tesla-SpaceX merger

Trump envoy floats Ukraine talks and summit with Putin and Xi

Italy’s buffalo mozzarella production grinds to a halt in truckers’ strike

item.title: Israel pushes to restart strikes against Iran

item.description:
The leaders of Ukraine, Finland and Norway hailed progress in talks in Oslo on Tuesday, SpaceX and Tesla are studying a merger, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing to restart large-scale strikes on Iran. Plus, UK gilts are catching back up with their peers after a sharp sell-off earlier this year.

item.title: Can Big Tech calm investors' AI jitters?
item.itunes:title: Can Big Tech calm investors' AI jitters?
item.itunes:subtitle: Credit default swaps are becoming a bellwether hedge for AI sentiment
item.description:
Protests across Europe over the high cost of living have turned increasingly disruptive, investors are racing to buy credit default swaps to protect their portfolios in the event the AI boom unravels, and Big Tech starts releasing their earnings reports this week. Plus, India’s second-richest man will try to pull off the country’s biggest initial public offering and Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship “Davos in the desert” investment conference following Houthi attacks.


Mentioned in this podcast:

French bond sell-off intensifies after violent protests

‘Cheap’ credit default swaps become bellwether hedge for AI sentiment

Ambani looks to pull off India’s biggest IPO

item.title: Martin Wolf on the US midterms: Is American democracy safe?
item.itunes:title: Martin Wolf on the US midterms: Is American democracy safe?
item.itunes:subtitle: Martin Wolf and former Republican adviser Robert Kagan on the stakes for US democracy
item.description:
As Americans prepare to vote in the November 3 midterm elections, FT chief economics commentator Martin Wolf asks what the result will mean for Donald Trump, the future of US democracy and America's place in the world. In the first of a six-part series of interviews with leading historians and political analysts, Martin speaks to the scholar and former Republican adviser Robert Kagan, who has spent a decade warning about Trump's authoritarian ambitions. They discuss how Trump has accumulated so much power, whether America's democratic institutions can still constrain him, and what might happen if Republicans lose control of Congress. Could these elections mark a turning point for American democracy or has the country already gone too far down the road towards authoritarianism?


Watch the full episode now on the FT’s main YouTube channel here: https://www.youtube.com/@FinancialTimes or search for ‘Martin Wolf on the World’, wherever you get your podcasts


Host: Martin Wolf

Producer: Mischa Frankl-Duval

Senior Producer: Laurence Knight
